action_criteria.expected_evidence: Six Rascovsky features from her husband's history with functional decline and an executive-predominant bedside profile
action_criteria.label: Structured informant history and bedside cognitive screen scored against the Rascovsky features
action_criteria.rationale: The diagnosis of bvFTD rests on the behavioural features obtained from an informant; here she minimises the changes and her husband gives the history.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe executive and social-cognition deficits with clinically significant apathy and disinhibition ratings and relatively preserved recognition memory and visuospatial function
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery including executive and social-cognition measures
action_criteria.rationale: Quantifies the executive and social-cognition profile and the relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, chemistry, liver tests, thyroid function, B12, folate and inflammatory markers; CK mildly raised at 318 U/L
action_criteria.label: Reversible-cause blood tests: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, ESR, CRP, with CK and liver tests
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory contributors before attributing decline to neurodegeneration; CK and liver tests are the baseline for the motor neuron disease work-up and for riluzole.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, left greater than right, with preserved hippocampal volume and posterior cortex
action_criteria.label: MRI brain without contrast, dementia protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Shows the frontal and anterior temporal atrophy pattern and excludes structural and vascular causes.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active and chronic denervation with fasciculation potentials in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles; normal motor conduction without conduction block and normal sensory studies
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reduced FVC (72% upright, 63% supine) and SNIP 52 cmH2O with MIP -44 cmH2O
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose the motor neuron disease. Once it is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left-predominant frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism or hypoperfusion with preserved posterior cortex
action_criteria.label: FDG-PET when the structural picture is unresolved
action_criteria.rationale: Frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism with posterior sparing supports FTD over AD; perfusion SPECT is the substitute where FDG-PET is unavailable. Here the MRI already shows the pattern.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansion; no other pathogenic variant on the panel
action_criteria.label: Genetic counselling and FTD-ALS gene panel (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT, SOD1, TARDBP) or FTD gene panel
action_criteria.rationale: A father with ALS at 58, a paternal aunt with behavioural dementia and an FTD-MND phenotype suggest an autosomal dominant FTD-ALS gene; testing follows counselling.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General criteria and FTD-MND overlap evidence only
action_criteria.label: Literature on bvFTD with motor neuron disease (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the criteria and on the FTD-MND overlap; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the fasciculations, cramps and EMG denervation to anxiety, deconditioning or benign fasciculation syndrome.
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition, falls and respiratory depression with inspiratory muscle weakness.
Do not pursue a myopathy work-up or muscle biopsy for the mildly raised CK: elevation of this degree is common with denervation.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of bvFTD with motor neuron disease (ALS-FTD): state the Rascovsky features present, the functional decline and the level of certainty, and the ALS evidence by Gold Coast 2020 (brisk jaw jerk, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann and Babinski signs with lower motor neuron involvement in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG); disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with her and her husband.

Explain why anxiety and benign fasciculation syndrome do not account for the syndrome: they cause neither upper motor neuron signs nor active denervation on EMG, and not progressive behavioural change with frontotemporal atrophy.

Refer to a specialist motor neuron disease multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy for speech and swallowing, dietetics with baseline weight, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), with caregiver education and support for her husband and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.

Discuss riluzole 50 mg twice daily with her and her husband; if it is started, measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter, stop it if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Arrange baseline respiratory assessment (FVC upright and supine, SNIP and MIP), refer to the respiratory/NIV service and discuss NIV once an AAN 2009 marker is met; if measured, the MIP of -44 cmH2O already meets one, so referral is due now. Assess orthopnoea and overnight oximetry or capnography to time NIV, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.
Address safety and capacity: driving (executive and motor impairment), finances and a lasting power of attorney while she can take part, and her work as an education coordinator.

Offer genetic counselling before any genetic test, given a father with ALS at 58 and a paternal aunt with behavioural dementia; discuss what a result would mean for her brother and two adult children, who may consider predictive testing only after their own counselling.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggests CJD or autoimmune encephalitis; neither is present here.
ECG has no role in the cognitive or neuromuscular workup of FTD-MND; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD-MND and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity to characterize frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; no parkinsonism or concern for PD/DLB/PSP is present; it is not indicated in FTD-MND.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD-MND diagnostic pathway.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia with motor neuron disease (FTD-MND)

differential.diagnosis: ALS with cognitive or behavioural impairment, without frontotemporal dementia
differential.key_features: Against: six Rascovsky features with loss of function and frontotemporal atrophy exceed the behavioural or cognitive impairment of ALS without dementia (Strong 2017).
Against: recognition memory preserved, normal hippocampi and posterior cortex, and motor neuron disease, which AD does not cause.

differential.diagnosis: Anxiety or depression as the sole explanation
differential.key_features: Against: no response to two antidepressant trials, progressive loss of function, objective executive and social-cognition deficits, and motor signs that psychiatric illness does not cause.
Against: weakness, upper motor neuron signs, and active denervation with chronic reinnervation in four regions on EMG.
Against: brisk jaw jerk, tongue fasciculations and bulbar denervation place the disease above the foramen magnum.

differential.diagnosis: Progressive supranuclear palsy with a frontal behavioural presentation
differential.key_features: Against: full eye movements, no early falls or axial rigidity, no midbrain atrophy, and lower motor neuron involvement.

key_clinical_evidence: Six Rascovsky features from her husband's history with functional decline and frontal and anterior temporal atrophy on MRI meet probable bvFTD.

Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann and Babinski signs with lower motor neuron involvement in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions; with bvFTD this is ALS-FTD (Strong 2017).
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy.
Anxiety and benign fasciculation syndrome do not cause upper motor neuron signs or active denervation; the earlier attribution delayed the diagnosis by 9 months.
CK 318 U/L (1.7x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

Reduced FVC (72% upright with a fall to 63% supine) and SNIP (52 cmH2O), with MIP -44 cmH2O. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry.
A father with ALS at 58 and a paternal aunt with behavioural dementia suggest an autosomal dominant FTD-ALS gene, most often C9orf72, and support offering genetic counselling.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anxiety does not cause tongue fasciculations, Babinski or Hoffmann signs, a brisk jaw jerk or active EMG denervation; the motor signs need electrodiagnostic evaluation regardless of the anxiety history.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder; primary care attribution of fasciculations and cramps to anxiety, deconditioning and benign fasciculation syndrome
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could anchor on anxiety as the explanation for twitching, cramps and fatigue, so that EMG is omitted and motor neuron disease missed.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild CK elevation is common with denervation; with upper motor neuron signs and widespread neurogenic change on EMG it does not suggest a primary myopathy.
red_herrings.data_point: CK mildly raised at 318 U/L (1.7x ULN)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could prompt a myopathy work-up (myositis panel, muscle biopsy) and divert attention from motor neuron disease.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: New disinhibition, loss of empathy, repetitive behaviour and dietary change with progressive functional decline are not features of depression; failure of two antidepressant trials calls for a neurodegenerative work-up.
red_herrings.data_point: Apathy and personality change treated as depression, with no response to two antidepressant trials
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could anchor on treatment-resistant depression and delay both the FTD evaluation and the neuromuscular work-up.

bvFTD with motor neuron disease.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. Up to about 15% of people with bvFTD develop motor neuron disease, most often with a C9orf72 expansion; electromyography establishes lower motor neuron involvement. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. V. is a 56-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman, a bilingual education coordinator, who presents to the cognitive neurology clinic accompanied by her husband. Her husband is the primary historian, as Ms. V. minimizes her difficulties and attributes them to stress and aging. Over the past 18 months, her husband has observed a profound personality transformation in a woman he describes as formerly warm, organized, and professionally accomplished. She has developed striking apathy — she stopped gardening (a lifelong passion), quit cooking family meals, and spends 6-8 hours per day passively watching television without responding to its content. She has become disinhibited: she laughed audibly at a family funeral, comments openly on strangers' physical appearance in public, and has made off-color remarks that are entirely out of character. She has lost empathy — when her husband was hospitalized briefly for a cardiac procedure 6 months ago, she showed no concern and did not call to check on him during the procedure. She repeats the same three anecdotes in nearly every conversation and asks the same questions repeatedly. She eats the same two meals in rotation and has developed a strong new preference for sweets (candy, pastries). She forgets recent conversations but recalls remote events in detail. She does not recognize that her behavior has changed and actively resists the idea that she needs evaluation.

Beyond the cognitive-behavioral changes, her husband notes she has been complaining of muscle twitching, cramps, and fatigue for 14 months. She stopped her daily 3-mile walks citing leg fatigue and cramps. Her speech has become subtly slurred, which she attributes to 'talking too fast.' She has had no falls but her husband has noticed she drags her left foot occasionally. These motor symptoms were evaluated by her primary care physician 9 months ago; he attributed them to anxiety, deconditioning, and possibly benign fasciculation syndrome given her anxiety history. He ordered routine labs and recommended therapy and magnesium supplementation.

Family history: her father died of ALS at age 58. Her paternal aunt developed behavioral changes in her early 60s and was diagnosed with dementia, dying in memory care. Her psychiatrist referred her to this clinic after noting that her apathy and personality change were not responsive to two antidepressant trials and were progressing. She has had no choking or coughing with meals, no weight loss and no breathlessness lying flat.

neurological_exam.additional: Her husband was present throughout and gave the collateral history. Weight stable at 64 kg.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements full with no nystagmus. Facial sensation symmetric. Facial activation symmetric. Tongue protrudes in midline, with fine fasciculations visible at rest; no tongue wasting. Palate elevation symmetric. Gag intact bilaterally. Mild slurring of rapid syllable repetition ('pa-ta-ka'), which she attributes to 'talking fast'. Jaw jerk mildly brisk.
neurological_exam.gait: Slightly wide-based, mildly spastic quality; drags the left foot intermittently. No cerebellar ataxia. Tandem gait impaired: 2 steps off-line and unable to complete 10 steps.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x3. Affect flat; makes two jokes at socially inappropriate moments during exam and shows no embarrassment when corrected.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal muscle bulk in upper extremities. Mild bilateral calf atrophy. Tone normal in upper limbs; no rigidity. Subtle increase in tone (catch) noted in bilateral hip flexors. Strength: deltoids 5/5, biceps 5/5, triceps 5/5, wrist extensors 5/5, intrinsics 4+/5 bilaterally. Hip flexors 4+/5 bilaterally. Tibialis anterior 4/5 bilaterally. Gastrocnemius 4+/5 bilaterally. Fasciculations visible in bilateral calves and right triceps at rest. Hoffmann's sign present bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 3+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 3+ bilaterally. Plantar responses: extensor (Babinski) bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in all four limbs.
